Energy markets are being reshaped as supply chains endure testing times

By Energy Connects

Sep 16, 2026

Today’s energy sector adaptability is a reflection of yesterday’s investment decisions.
This was one of the key messages from an influential Gastech panel discussion that asked whether energy markets were ending in favour of strategic blocs.
H.E. Jassim AlShirawi, Secretary General, International Energy Forum (IEF), argued that disruptions in the Middle East demonstrated the adaptability of energy markets and the importance of timely investment across all fuels and supply chains.
“I don’t think the energy markets are ending,” he told the Exchange Theatre. “They are actually rather adapting because of geopolitics, strategic competition and energy security concerns.
“And with recent disruptions we have witnessed … they have shown and demonstrated the ability of energy markets to respond,” said AlShirawi as part of the executive session, ‘The end of the energy market? Are we in the age of the strategic bloc?’
“Organisations like us and many stakeholders, we always call for adequate and timely investment in all forms of energy and fuels and across the supply chain in order to improve resilience and to ensure supply for meeting growing future energy demand, and also any potential future disruptions.”
The IEF and other organisations are calling for more collaboration to stave off what AlShirawi called “informational choke points where information is not available for decision-makers”.
“Transparency in the energy market is essential. Data about production levels, about spare capacity, investment, infrastructure, all are very important in order to make timely interventions.”
On the geopolitical angle, Derek Grossman, Founder & Chief Analyst, Indo-Pacific Solutions, said he wasn’t seeing countries across his region aligning with either the US or China, but “quite the opposite”.
“The Strait of Hormuz situation underscores that point. What we have seen is countries are finding within themselves resilience to withstand the pressures of the war, whether that means switching fuels, relying on different forms of energy within their countries, interacting with some of their friends, and rivals in some cases, in order to secure energy reserves in spite of, maybe, political differences.”

Shehryar Omar, CEO, Petroleum Institute of Pakistan, agreed that recent events have seen nations prioritise pragmatism over ideology, such as Germany restarting coal plants.
“It’s not that the energy market has ended, but the energy marketplace, as we have known it for 50 years, has been completely scrambled,” he said.
“Part of it is because of electrification, but one of the main things that’s happened in the last six months is that ideologies that used to drive relationships are kind of going by the wayside, and people are saying, ‘what’s the most practical thing for my country, for my people?”
As Secretary General of the East Mediterranean Gas Forum, Osama Mobarez sometimes brings together politically opposed actors around the common interest of energy.
“What’s happening makes it quite difficult for any country alone to navigate this,” he said.
“We saw an opportunity for resources that cannot be developed due to several challenges, whether lack of markets, lack of infrastructure, and at the same time there are countries who have the markets or the infrastructure.

“So how can we bring those countries and governments together to generate value and share this value?
“Maybe for the first time we can see energy from a different perspective. Maybe we can have energy as some sort of a prelude to political alignment and mutual interests in energy. Maybe it can bring countries together.
“I look at it not as coalitions and blocs; I look at it more from the energy security perspective. What is available for each country? You cannot diversify without managing and working out the geopolitics.”
Omar reiterated the market has “definitely changed”. He added: “I don’t think we’re going back to the same thing after Hormuz reopens because people are scared it can happen again.
“Energy security means food security and, especially for countries with large, poor populations, food security is as important as anything else.”
